 Print this Article 
 View Comments Hiker Jodi Cobourn under the “Mysterious Hanging Boulder” on Sept. 19. Courtesy Charlie Worthen After more than a century at Polar Caves Park, a historic, 80-ton boulder fell at the popular tourist site in New Hampshire on Sunday, the last day of the season. 
 The tourist site in Rumney announced the news Monday. “We are incredibly grateful no one was injured in the incident,” park management said in a statement posted on its website . 
 The “Mysterious Hanging Boulder” was just above hikers’ heads as they traversed a stretch of trail at the park. Nobody was in its path when it came crashing down, the statement said. 
 The boulder had held its spot for the 104 years of the park’s existence, officials wrote in a social media post. 
 But the famous granite boulder was deposited in its hanging position by a glacier thousands of years ago, just like many boulders across the state, said Joe Licciardi, a professor of glacial geology at the University of New Hampshire. 
 Get N.H. Morning Report A weekday newsletter delivering the N.H. news you need to know right to your inbox. Enter Email Sign Up “The Polar Caves are actually called that because the caves are spaces between enormous granite boulders that were at one point put there by glaciers,” said Licciardi, 56. 
 The enormous boulder that fell Sunday had been balanced in place, with some of its weight resting on its base and some hanging over the trail, said Jan Earle, a geologist who has worked with the US Geological Survey and state parks across the country. 
 “It was a balanced rock essentially, so if more of its weight was hanging over the edge than sitting on its base, then it was just a matter of time until gravity and erosion of its base took over, and it tipped over,” said Earle, 79. 
 Over time, it likely succumbed to a mix of geologic factors. 
 A combination of wind and rain eroding support underneath the boulder and the “weight of water, dust or other rocks falling on top of it” could have tipped the balance, she said. 
 “It’s just been sitting there for a long time, and it’s sort of like a old car rusting and then finally falling apart,” Earle said. 
 Licciardi said the boulder could have been vulnerable to erosion caused by water freezing and thawing. When water turns to ice, he said, its volume expands by roughly 9 percent. 
 “That’s more than enough to cause the rock to further fracture and crumble,” he said. 
 A safety assessment will be conducted during the park’s offseason. 
 “The safety of our guests and employees continues to be our highest priority,” the park stated. 
 A video of the aftermath captured by one hiker and posted online showed a railing for the trail’s wooden walkway smashed to pieces, with access to the rest of the trail cut off by the boulder, which now sits upright on its side. 
 In the corner of the video, a trail sign that had identified the rock overhang with an arrow now gestured to empty air. 
 “This boulder is cracked all the way through and rests on 3 contact points in the back,” the sign read. “It weighs 80 tons, 75 percent of which is hanging over your head.” 
 The Polar Caves, which features nine granite caves to explore across roughly 2 miles, opened in 1922, according to its website . Other cave areas along the trail course feature such names as “The Lemon Squeeze,” “Devil’s Turnpike,” and “Fat Man’s Misery.” 
 Park officials declined to comment further on what may have caused the boulder to fall. 
 In 2003, residents were stunned when the Old Man of the Mountain, a New Hampshire geographic landmark, crumbled and collapsed , plunging from the side of Cannon Mountain in Franconia Notch State Park. 
 New Hampshire's iconic Old Man of the Mountain, seen in an archive photo taken Oct. 2, 2001 (left) and after the 40-foot-tall face had collapsed on May 3, 2003. Associated Press The outcropping, which looked like a human face in profile, consisted of five granite cliff ledges and was a beloved state symbol, appearing on license plates and New Hampshire’s commemorative quarter. 
 The May 3 collapse was also caused by apparent natural geological forces, causing a rock slide on the side of the mountain, the Globe reported in 2003. 
 The massive rocks that composed the Old Man’s prominent “forehead” and “nose” tumbled toward Profile Lake, 1,200 feet below, stopping short of the water. The “face” spanned 40 feet from top to tip, but only the 12 bottom feet remained after the rock slide, officials said at the time.
